stem: Which statement best describes the Task table in the Now Platform?

options.text: A base table that holds fields common to all work items (number, state, assigned_to, priority, etc.) from which Incident, Change, Problem, and many other tables extend.
A read-only audit log of every user action across the platform.
A table containing only scheduled jobs.
A reporting view across Incidents and Changes that doesn't store data of its own.

rationale: Task is the parent table for work items in the platform. Incident, Change, Problem, and many other tables extend it, which is why they share fields like number, state, assigned_to, and short_description.

distractor_notes.B: Audit history lives in audit tables, not on the Task table.
distractor_notes.C: Scheduled jobs live on sys_trigger, not on Task.
distractor_notes.D: Task is a real table, not a virtual report view.

stem: What is table extension in the Now Platform?

options.text: A relationship where a child table inherits the fields and behavior of a parent table and can add its own.
A read replica of the table maintained for reporting.
A foreign key constraint between two unrelated tables.
A scheduled job that copies records from one table to another.

rationale: Table extension is inheritance for tables. A child table inherits every field defined on the parent and can layer on its own. Incident, Change, and Problem all extend Task, which is why they share core fields.

distractor_notes.B: Replicas are an infrastructure concept; extension is a data-model concept.
distractor_notes.C: Foreign keys connect rows, not table definitions.
distractor_notes.D: Scheduled copies aren't how the platform shares schema.

stem: Which of these tables does NOT extend Task in a standard ServiceNow instance?

options.text: incident
change_request
problem
sys_user

rationale: sys_user is the users table — completely separate from the Task hierarchy. Incident, Change Request, and Problem all extend Task and share its common fields.

distractor_notes.B: Change Request extends Task.
distractor_notes.C: Problem extends Task.

stem: Which of the following fields is inherited from the Task table by all extending tables like Incident, Change, and Problem?

options.text: assigned_to
caller_id
model_id
ci_class

rationale: assigned_to is defined on the Task base table, so every extending table inherits it. That's why incidents, changes, and problems all share a consistent way to express ownership.

distractor_notes.B: caller_id is specific to Incident.
distractor_notes.C: model_id appears on CI/asset tables, not on Task.
distractor_notes.D: ci_class isn't a Task field.

stem: An admin wants assignment_group and assigned_to to behave consistently — picking a group filters the assignable users to members of that group. Which platform feature enables this out-of-the-box?

options.text: A reference qualifier on assigned_to that constrains it to the selected assignment_group's members.
An ACL that prevents users from being assigned.
A scheduled job that runs every 15 minutes to fix invalid assignments.
A workflow that emails the admin when assignments don't match.

rationale: Reference qualifiers narrow which records a reference field can pick. The platform's out-of-the-box qualifier on assigned_to looks at the chosen assignment_group and limits the user list to that group's members.

distractor_notes.B: ACLs are about access, not filtering field values.
distractor_notes.C: Cleaning up bad data after the fact is a workaround, not a constraint.
distractor_notes.D: Email alerts catch problems late — the qualifier prevents them in the first place.

stem: Most child tables of Task share a common state-progression pattern. Which statement best describes that pattern?

options.text: Records progress through a defined sequence of states such as New → In Progress → Resolved → Closed, with state values stored as integers on a choice list field.
State is a free-text field on every record.
State is computed at runtime from the record's age.
State is stored in localStorage in the user's browser.

rationale: Task and its children use a choice list for state, stored as integers, that walks through a defined lifecycle (e.g., New, In Progress, On Hold, Resolved, Closed). Each child table can tailor labels and add states, but the pattern is consistent.

distractor_notes.B: Free-text states would defeat reporting and automation. State is a choice field.
distractor_notes.C: State doesn't auto-compute from age. SLA timers can use age, but the state field itself is explicit.
distractor_notes.D: Record state is server-side data, not browser storage.

stem: A user opens an incident and notices a Parent field. What is the typical use of that field?

options.text: To link this task to another task that contains it or that this task is part of, expressing a parent–child relationship between work items.
To set the user's manager on the record.
To select the previous record number in number sequence.
To assign the record to the parent company.

rationale: The Parent field on Task lets you link records into a parent–child relationship — useful for grouping related incidents, tying child changes to a parent change, or building task breakdowns.

distractor_notes.B: User management lives on sys_user via the manager field, not on the task's Parent.
distractor_notes.C: Parent isn't a numbering link; numbers come from the number maintenance settings.
distractor_notes.D: Company assignment lives on dedicated fields, not Parent.

stem: What does the Activity Log on a task record typically show?

options.text: A chronological feed of field changes, comments, work notes, and notifications associated with the record.
Only the comments the caller has typed.
Only the work notes the assignee has typed.
A list of database connections used while the record was open.

rationale: The Activity Log/Stream is a unified chronological feed on the record — field changes, work notes, comments, attachments, and notification events all flow through it. It's the record's narrative.

distractor_notes.B: Comments are visible to end users; work notes are internal. Both appear in the activity feed, plus other events.
distractor_notes.C: Same as above — both are present.
distractor_notes.D: Database connection events don't live on the record.

stem: On a typical incident, what's the difference between Work notes and Comments?

options.text: Work notes are intended for internal team communication; Comments (additional comments) are visible to the customer/end user.
They're identical — the platform stores both in the same field.
Work notes are visible to everyone; Comments are admin-only.
Work notes can only be entered through email; Comments only through the form.

rationale: Work notes are internal-only collaboration. Comments (often labeled 'Additional comments') are intended to be visible to the customer through the portal or notifications. Knowing which is which prevents accidental customer-facing snark.

distractor_notes.B: They're separate fields with different visibility semantics.
distractor_notes.C: Backwards. Work notes are internal; comments are customer-visible.
distractor_notes.D: Both can be entered through the form or through inbound email.

stem: A developer wants to add a custom field that should appear on every task-derived table (Incident, Change, Problem, etc.). Where should they add the field?

options.text: On the Task table — extending tables inherit it automatically.
On each child table individually.
Only on the Incident table.
On the sys_user table.

rationale: Adding the field once on Task lets every extending table inherit it for free. That's the whole point of table extension — share schema where it belongs in the hierarchy.

distractor_notes.B: Adding the same field on every child is repetitive and easy to get out of sync.
distractor_notes.C: Only Incident would have it; other task tables wouldn't.
distractor_notes.D: sys_user is unrelated to tasks.

stem: Why do incidents have numbers like INC0010023, changes like CHG0001234, and problems like PRB0040001 instead of plain integers?

options.text: Each task-derived table has its own number-maintenance configuration (prefix + counter) so records are distinguishable across the platform.
The numbers are encrypted versions of the record's sys_id.
The numbers are randomly generated UUIDs.
The numbers are computed from the assigned_to user's employee ID.

rationale: Each task-derived table has its own number-maintenance configuration: a prefix (INC, CHG, PRB, etc.) and a numeric counter. That's why tasks of different types are immediately readable at a glance.

distractor_notes.B: sys_id is a separate 32-character GUID; the visible number is independent.
distractor_notes.C: Numbers are sequential per table, not random.
distractor_notes.D: Assignee identity has nothing to do with the record number.

stem: A change request requires approval from two managers in sequence before it can proceed. Which platform mechanism is designed for this approval routing?

options.text: Approval records (sysapproval_approver) generated by a flow or workflow attached to the change process, ordered sequentially.
Two separate incident records, one per approver.
An ACL that requires two field updates to save the record.
A UI policy that hides the Save button until both managers comment.

rationale: Approvals on tasks are tracked on sysapproval_approver and orchestrated by the change process — typically a flow or workflow that creates approval requests in a defined order. That's how multi-step approval is meant to work.

distractor_notes.B: Creating sibling incidents loses the parent–child relationship and the ordered approval semantics.
distractor_notes.C: ACLs are about who can save, not who has signed off.
distractor_notes.D: Hiding Save doesn't track who approved, when, or why.

stem: What is the primary purpose of Incident Management in ITSM?

options.text: Restore normal service operation as quickly as possible after an unplanned interruption or reduction in quality.
Plan and approve changes to production infrastructure.
Identify the underlying cause of recurring service issues.
Track the long-term lifecycle of physical assets.

rationale: Incident Management exists to restore service as fast as possible. It's about minimizing impact to the business, not about finding root cause (that's Problem) or planning changes (that's Change).

distractor_notes.B: Planning and approving changes is Change Management.
distractor_notes.C: Identifying root cause is Problem Management.
distractor_notes.D: Tracking physical assets is Asset/HAM.

stem: Which of these is the typical default sequence of incident states?

options.text: New → In Progress → On Hold → Resolved → Closed
Draft → Submitted → Approved → Implemented
Created → Reviewed → Published → Retired
Logged → Investigated → Eradicated → Recovered

rationale: Out-of-the-box, incidents move through New → In Progress → On Hold (optional) → Resolved → Closed. Customers and reporting depend on this consistent flow.

distractor_notes.B: That's closer to a Change Request flow, not incidents.
distractor_notes.C: That's closer to a Knowledge article lifecycle.
distractor_notes.D: Those terms describe a security-incident response model, not the standard ITSM incident state model.

stem: How is incident Priority typically derived out-of-the-box?

options.text: From a Priority Lookup that combines Impact and Urgency into a single priority value.
Manually typed by the caller into a free-text field.
From the geographic location of the assignee.
From the most recently committed update set.

rationale: Out-of-the-box, Impact × Urgency drives Priority through a Priority Lookup matrix. Setting impact and urgency on a new incident makes priority calculate automatically.

distractor_notes.B: Priority is a choice list. It's not a free-text typed by callers.
distractor_notes.C: Assignee location doesn't drive priority.
distractor_notes.D: Update sets are unrelated to operational data calculation.

stem: Which Change Management type is intended for low-risk, pre-approved, repeatable changes?

options.text: Standard
Normal
Emergency
Major

rationale: Standard changes are pre-approved, well-understood, low-risk changes that follow a template. They skip heavy approval and CAB review because the template was already vetted.

distractor_notes.B: Normal changes require CAB review and typical approval — not pre-approved.
distractor_notes.C: Emergency changes are for urgent issues that can't wait for normal review.
distractor_notes.D: Major isn't a standard change type label in OOB Change Management.

stem: Which Change Management type is intended for unplanned, time-critical changes — for example, a production outage requiring an immediate fix?

options.text: Emergency
Standard
Normal
Routine

rationale: Emergency changes are designed for urgent fixes that can't wait for the normal CAB cycle. They still have an approval path, but on an accelerated timeline.

distractor_notes.B: Standard changes are pre-approved, low-risk — the opposite of unplanned and time-critical.
distractor_notes.C: Normal changes follow the full review cycle, which won't fit an outage timeline.
distractor_notes.D: 'Routine' isn't a change type in OOB Change Management.

stem: A team frequently performs the same database patch every Tuesday with no incidents. Which change type best fits this work?

options.text: Create a Standard Change Template for the patch and submit the change against it.
Submit a brand-new Normal change each Tuesday.
Submit an Emergency change each Tuesday.
Submit an incident each Tuesday.

rationale: Recurring, low-risk, well-understood work is exactly the use case for a Standard Change Template. The template gets pre-approved once; each weekly execution is a Standard change created from the template.

distractor_notes.B: Submitting a fresh Normal change every week wastes CAB cycles.
distractor_notes.C: Emergencies are for unplanned urgent fixes, not for routine recurring work.
distractor_notes.D: An incident is for restoring service after an unplanned interruption.

stem: What is the primary purpose of Problem Management?

options.text: Identify the underlying cause of incidents and prevent recurrence.
Restore service as fast as possible after an interruption.
Track planned changes to infrastructure.
Approve user access to applications.

rationale: Problem Management investigates root cause to stop incidents from recurring. Incidents fix today; problems fix tomorrow.

distractor_notes.B: Restoring service is Incident Management.
distractor_notes.C: Tracking changes is Change Management.
distractor_notes.D: Access approvals are part of identity/access governance, not Problem.

stem: Three different customers logged incidents about the same authentication failure over the last week. What's the appropriate next step in ITSM terms?

options.text: Open a Problem record, link the related incidents to it, and investigate root cause.
Merge all three incidents into one and close the others as duplicates without further investigation.
Open three separate Change records.
Send each caller an apology email and close the incidents.

rationale: Recurring incidents pointing at the same underlying issue is the canonical signal to open a Problem and link the affected incidents to it. The problem owns the root-cause investigation while incidents continue to track service restoration.

distractor_notes.B: Merging doesn't address recurrence. Closing as duplicate hides the pattern.
distractor_notes.C: Changes are planned modifications. They aren't the right artifact for investigating a recurring failure.
distractor_notes.D: Apologizing and closing leaves the underlying defect unresolved.

stem: An incident and a problem are most usefully distinguished by which idea?

options.text: An incident records a service-affecting event needing restoration; a problem investigates the underlying cause to prevent recurrence.
An incident is small; a problem is large.
An incident is internal; a problem is customer-facing.
An incident is open longer than a problem.

rationale: Scope matters less than purpose. An incident is 'restore service.' A problem is 'why did this happen and how do we stop it from happening again.' Two different jobs, often handled by two different teams.

distractor_notes.B: Size doesn't define the distinction. A 'large' incident is still about restoration.
distractor_notes.C: Both can be internal or external — they're not separated by audience.
distractor_notes.D: Problems frequently outlive incidents. Duration isn't the defining quality.

stem: A Normal change is in 'Assess' state. The CAB has reviewed it. What state transition typically follows next?

options.text: Authorize — the change is approved and ready to be scheduled for implementation.
Closed — the change is finished without implementation.
Resolved — the change is reverted.
Cancelled — the change is automatically deleted.

rationale: After Assess, an approved Normal change moves to Authorize, then Scheduled, Implement, Review, and Closed. Authorize is the next state when CAB has signed off.

distractor_notes.B: Closing immediately skips implementation — that's a separate flow if the change is withdrawn.
distractor_notes.C: Resolved isn't part of the Change state model in this way; Resolved belongs to Incident.
distractor_notes.D: Cancelled is an explicit choice, not automatic, and doesn't delete the record.

stem: An incident is resolved. Which condition typically must be true before the platform moves it to Closed?

options.text: A defined auto-close interval passes after Resolved without reopening, or the caller confirms resolution — per the configured policy.
The instance restarts.
An admin manually edits the sys_id.
Every related KB article is republished.

rationale: The configured auto-close behavior (e.g., 7 days after Resolved) or explicit caller confirmation moves an incident from Resolved to Closed. The platform won't close active incidents on its own.

distractor_notes.B: Instance restarts have nothing to do with record state.
distractor_notes.C: Editing sys_id is not a supported operation.
distractor_notes.D: Knowledge republishing isn't a prerequisite for closing incidents.

stem: What is the primary role of the Change Advisory Board (CAB) in ITSM?

options.text: A cross-functional group that reviews and authorizes proposed Normal changes and assesses risk and scheduling.
A team that resolves incidents at the service desk.
A monitoring tool that watches for unauthorized changes.
A scheduled job that auto-approves all standard changes weekly.

rationale: The Change Advisory Board reviews Normal changes — assessing risk, impact, scheduling conflicts — and authorizes them to proceed. CAB is people and process, not a tool.

distractor_notes.B: Service desk handles incidents, not change authorization.
distractor_notes.C: CAB isn't a monitoring tool. Drift detection is a separate discipline.
distractor_notes.D: Auto-approval isn't CAB's job; pre-approved Standard changes are a different model.

stem: What is the primary purpose of Knowledge Management in the Now Platform?

options.text: Capture, organize, share, and reuse information through knowledge articles so users and agents can find answers faster.
Track the financial value of IT assets over time.
Plan and approve infrastructure changes.
Replace incident records with KB articles.

rationale: Knowledge Management is about storing reusable information — how-tos, FAQs, runbooks — in knowledge articles so callers and agents can find answers quickly. Done well, it shifts work from tickets to self-service.

distractor_notes.B: Asset financial tracking is Asset Management.
distractor_notes.C: Change planning is Change Management.
distractor_notes.D: KB articles complement incidents; they don't replace them.

stem: What is a Knowledge Base (KB) in the Now Platform?

options.text: A container that holds related knowledge articles and has its own ownership, workflow, and access controls.
A field on every incident record that stores text.
A row on sys_user holding the user's reading preferences.
A type of dashboard widget.

rationale: A Knowledge Base is the container — a logical grouping (IT, HR, Customer Service, etc.) with its own owners, workflow, and access rules. Articles live inside a KB and inherit some of that governance.

distractor_notes.B: Knowledge isn't a free-text field on incidents.
distractor_notes.C: User preferences live on sys_user but they aren't KBs.
distractor_notes.D: Dashboards have widgets — a KB isn't one.

stem: Which lifecycle states are typical for a knowledge article from authoring to retirement?

options.text: Draft → Review → Published → Retired.
New → In Progress → Resolved → Closed.
Open → Authorized → Implemented → Reviewed.
Created → Verified → Encrypted → Backed Up.

rationale: KB articles typically move through Draft (author), Review (approval), Published (visible), and Retired (no longer current). The workflow is configurable but those four are the classic stages.

distractor_notes.B: That's the Incident state model.
distractor_notes.C: That's closer to Change Management.
distractor_notes.D: Encryption and backup aren't article states.

stem: What is the role of User Criteria in Knowledge Management?

options.text: Define who can or cannot read or contribute to a KB or article based on attributes like role, group, department, location, or company.
Filter the list of incidents shown on the agent home page.
Define which fields appear on a form.
Schedule recurring publication of articles.

rationale: User Criteria define audience for knowledge — Can Read, Cannot Read, Can Contribute, Cannot Contribute — based on user attributes. They're the supported way to scope visibility and contribution without writing custom ACLs.

distractor_notes.B: Incident list filtering uses list filters and assignment, not user criteria.
distractor_notes.C: Form layout is controlled by Form Designer/Layout, not user criteria.
distractor_notes.D: Article scheduling is part of the workflow, not user criteria.

stem: An HR KB should be visible only to HR employees and contractors should be excluded. How is this typically configured?

options.text: Add a 'Can Read' user criteria that includes the HR group and a 'Cannot Read' user criteria that excludes contractors on the HR KB.
Encrypt every HR article with a password.
Write a UI policy that hides HR articles from contractors.
Move HR articles to a hidden URL that contractors don't know about.

rationale: User Criteria handle exactly this case: Can Read narrows audience to HR; Cannot Read excludes contractors. The KB itself enforces the rule centrally instead of scattering logic across the platform.

distractor_notes.B: Article-level password encryption isn't the platform's access model.
distractor_notes.C: UI policies don't gate visibility outside the form context — they don't apply to portal search or KB lookups.
distractor_notes.D: Security through obscurity isn't security.

stem: An agent wants to create a brand new knowledge article from a resolved incident. Which feature is intended for this?

options.text: Use the 'Create Knowledge' / 'Post Knowledge' action on the incident, which seeds a draft article using fields from the incident.
Manually copy/paste the incident's description into a new browser tab and email it to the KB team.
Mark the incident as 'is_knowledge_article = true' on sys_dictionary.
Export the incident as a PDF and attach it to a new KB record.

rationale: Out-of-the-box, agents can trigger article creation directly from a resolved incident. The platform seeds a draft using fields from the source record so knowledge capture happens in the flow of work.

distractor_notes.B: Manual copy/paste defeats the integration the platform provides.
distractor_notes.C: sys_dictionary defines fields, not record state.
distractor_notes.D: PDFs make poor reusable articles. Attachments aren't articles.

stem: Which statement about knowledge article versioning is most accurate?

options.text: When an article is updated through the supported workflow, the platform can produce a new version, preserving the prior version for reference.
Articles cannot be versioned — every edit overwrites the previous content irretrievably.
Versions are stored in the user's browser localStorage.
Versioning requires a third-party plugin from the App Store.

rationale: Knowledge supports versioning so an edit can produce a new version while keeping the prior one for history and rollback. Whether versioning is on depends on KB configuration, but it's a platform capability.

distractor_notes.B: Edits don't have to be destructive when versioning is configured.
distractor_notes.C: Articles live in the database, not in the browser.
distractor_notes.D: Versioning isn't a third-party add-on.

stem: Why might an organization use multiple Knowledge Bases instead of one large KB?

options.text: To separate ownership, workflows, access, and category trees by audience (e.g., IT, HR, Customer Service).
ServiceNow requires a separate KB per article author.
Each KB stores articles on its own physical server.
Multiple KBs are required for performance — a single KB cannot index more than 100 articles.

rationale: Multiple KBs let different teams own their content, run their own approval workflow, set audience-specific access, and organize their own categories. It's an organizational model, not a performance constraint.

distractor_notes.B: There's no per-author KB requirement.
distractor_notes.C: KBs don't map to physical servers.
distractor_notes.D: There's no 100-article limit.

stem: How is a knowledge article typically organized inside a Knowledge Base?

options.text: Articles are placed in categories (and optional subcategories) within a KB, supporting hierarchical browsing alongside search.
Articles are sorted only by ascending sys_id.
Articles must be filed under exactly one tag — no categories exist.
Articles are organized by the user who opened them most recently.

rationale: Knowledge uses a category (and optional subcategory) tree inside each KB for hierarchical organization. Users can browse by category or search across the whole KB.

distractor_notes.B: sys_id ordering wouldn't be useful for end users.
distractor_notes.C: Tags can apply, but categories also exist and are the main organizational unit.
distractor_notes.D: Viewing history is per-user and isn't how articles are filed.

stem: What is the role of article feedback (helpful/not helpful ratings, comments) in Knowledge Management?

options.text: It provides signals that owners use to improve, update, or retire articles based on reader experience.
It is purely cosmetic — feedback is never stored on the platform.
It automatically deletes any article that receives negative feedback.
It increases an article's sys_id.

rationale: Feedback exists to inform article owners. Patterns of low ratings or comments highlight articles that need rewriting, updating, or retirement.

distractor_notes.B: Feedback is stored, reported on, and used in governance.
distractor_notes.C: Negative feedback prompts review, not auto-deletion.
distractor_notes.D: sys_id is immutable. Feedback never changes it.

stem: An admin wants every article in the HR KB to be approved by an HR Knowledge Manager before it goes Published. What's the most appropriate configuration?

options.text: Configure or assign a knowledge workflow on the HR KB that requires manager approval before transitioning to Published.
Mark the KB as private and tell HR managers to read every article over email.
Disable Knowledge Management on the instance.
Delete the Draft state from the article form layout.

rationale: Each KB can be configured with its own workflow. Adding a manager approval step in the HR KB's workflow enforces sign-off before Published — no ad-hoc email reviews required.

distractor_notes.B: Email reviews aren't auditable and don't enforce the workflow.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling KM globally breaks the use case.
distractor_notes.D: Hiding the Draft state doesn't introduce approval — it removes a state from the UI.

stem: An article references a process that has since been deprecated. What's the right action?

options.text: Move the article to Retired state so it's no longer surfaced to users while preserving the record for history.
Delete the article from the database immediately.
Open an incident on the article.
Mark the article as a duplicate of itself.

rationale: Retiring is the right move: the article stops appearing in search and browse, but the record remains for audit and historical reference. Deletion loses that history.

distractor_notes.B: Hard-deleting articles erases history and any links pointing to them.
distractor_notes.C: Incidents track service interruptions, not stale content.
distractor_notes.D: Self-duplication isn't a meaningful state.

stem: What is the primary purpose of Service Catalog?

options.text: Present a structured set of orderable services and request items to end users, with workflows that fulfill those requests behind the scenes.
Replace the Incident Management app entirely.
Store the company's marketing materials.
Hold every record on the platform in one searchable list.

rationale: Service Catalog is the storefront — users browse and order items (a laptop, software access, an HR change), and the platform spins up the appropriate fulfillment workflow. Self-service in, automation behind.

distractor_notes.B: Incidents and catalog requests are separate, complementary apps.
distractor_notes.C: Marketing content lives elsewhere (Knowledge, CMS, etc.).
distractor_notes.D: Catalog isn't a unified list of all platform records.

stem: What is a Catalog Item?

options.text: An orderable thing in the catalog (laptop, access request, name change, etc.) with its own variables, workflow, and price/category.
A free-text field on an incident form.
A scheduled job that polls inventory.
A row on sys_user.

rationale: A catalog item represents one orderable thing. It carries variables (what to ask the user), a workflow or flow (how to fulfill it), and metadata (category, image, price, who can see it).

distractor_notes.B: It's a discrete configuration object, not a free-text field.
distractor_notes.C: Catalog items aren't scheduled jobs.
distractor_notes.D: sys_user rows are users. Catalog items live on their own table.

stem: What are catalog Variables used for?

options.text: They define the questions asked of the requester on a catalog item (text, choice, reference, etc.) and capture the answers used by the fulfillment workflow.
They are server-side global JavaScript variables shared across all scripts on the instance.
They store the user's session timeout.
They cache outbound email templates.

rationale: Variables are the form fields on a catalog item — what the platform asks the requester. The answers flow into the requested item record and feed the fulfillment workflow.

distractor_notes.B: Catalog variables are specific to a catalog item, not platform-wide JS.
distractor_notes.C: Session timeout is a system property.
distractor_notes.D: Email templates live in the notifications subsystem.

stem: When a user submits a catalog item, what records does the platform typically create?

options.text: A Request (REQ) header record and one or more Requested Item (RITM) records, often with one or more Catalog Tasks (SCTASK) generated by the workflow.
Only an Incident record.
Only a Change record.
Only a Problem record.

rationale: Submission creates a Request (REQ) as the umbrella, a Requested Item (RITM) per item ordered, and Catalog Tasks (SCTASK) generated by the fulfillment workflow as work to do.

distractor_notes.B: Incidents are about unplanned service interruptions, not catalog orders.
distractor_notes.C: Changes are planned infrastructure modifications, not request fulfillment.
distractor_notes.D: Problems track root cause investigations.

stem: An admin wants to surface only a subset of catalog items to a partner company, not the full company catalog. Which mechanism is most appropriate?

options.text: Use User Criteria on the relevant catalog items / categories to control who sees them.
Create a duplicate of every internal item and rename them.
Hide items with a CSS rule on the portal.
Delete the items that shouldn't be visible.

rationale: User Criteria control audience for catalog items and categories — exactly the same mechanism Knowledge uses. Add a Can View criteria for the partner audience; deny on the rest.

distractor_notes.B: Duplicating items inflates maintenance and drifts the two copies over time.
distractor_notes.C: CSS hides things visually but doesn't enforce access — a savvy user could still submit by URL.
distractor_notes.D: Deletion removes items entirely; the goal is selective visibility.

stem: What is a Category in Service Catalog?

options.text: A grouping that organizes catalog items under a heading users can browse (e.g., Hardware, Software, HR).
A workflow stage on a Requested Item.
A role attached to a user.
A type of attachment.

rationale: Categories organize catalog items into browsable groupings. They give the catalog its shape and help users find what they need without scrolling endlessly.

distractor_notes.B: Workflow stages live on the fulfillment flow, not categories.
distractor_notes.C: Categories aren't roles.
distractor_notes.D: Categories aren't attachments.

stem: What is a Variable Set?

options.text: A reusable group of variables (with their order, layout, and behavior) that can be attached to multiple catalog items.
A read-only field on the requested item.
A user's saved cart in the portal.
A set of audit records for variable changes.

rationale: Variable sets are reusable bundles of variables. Define once, attach to many catalog items — useful for shared inputs like 'requested for, location, justification.'

distractor_notes.B: Variables are inputs, not read-only display values.
distractor_notes.C: Saved carts are a portal feature, not variable sets.
distractor_notes.D: Audits aren't variable sets.

stem: After a user submits a 'New Laptop' catalog item, the workflow generates two catalog tasks: one for IT to provision the laptop and one for Finance to record the asset. Which record type are these tasks?

options.text: SCTASK (Catalog Task) records.
INC (Incident) records.
CHG (Change Request) records.
KB (Knowledge) records.

rationale: Tasks generated by a catalog fulfillment workflow are SCTASK records (Catalog Tasks). They give each team a discrete unit of work tied back to the requesting RITM and REQ.

distractor_notes.B: Incidents are for service interruptions, not catalog fulfillment.
distractor_notes.C: Changes are for planned modifications — not for routine provisioning tasks.
distractor_notes.D: KBs are knowledge articles.

stem: On a catalog item, an admin wants the 'Justification' variable to appear only when 'Request type' is set to 'Above standard equipment.' Which configuration is intended for this?

options.text: A Catalog UI Policy on the item that sets Justification to visible/mandatory based on Request type.
A regular Business Rule on the requested item table.
An ACL on the variable.
A scheduled job that toggles visibility every minute.

rationale: Catalog UI Policies are the catalog-side cousin of regular UI Policies. They drive show/hide, mandatory, and read-only behavior on catalog variables based on other variable values. Exactly this use case.

distractor_notes.B: Business rules run server-side and aren't the right tool for conditional variable display.
distractor_notes.C: ACLs are about access, not conditional visibility on the catalog form.
distractor_notes.D: Scheduled jobs are wildly the wrong mechanism for UI behavior.

stem: An admin needs to onboard a new hire with a laptop, a phone, software access, and an HR profile all in one go. Which catalog construct bundles related items into a single ordering experience?

options.text: An Order Guide that gathers shared inputs once and then submits multiple related catalog items together.
A single mega catalog item with one workflow that does everything.
A KB article that lists the steps.
Four separate incidents.

rationale: Order Guides are designed for exactly this: collect a small set of shared questions (employee name, start date, location), then submit a bundle of catalog items in one flow. The user gets one experience; the platform gets discrete fulfillable items.

distractor_notes.B: A mega item buries discrete fulfillment work in one record and makes routing harder.
distractor_notes.C: A KB article is documentation, not a bundling mechanism.
distractor_notes.D: Incidents aren't catalog requests.

stem: An admin wants the fulfillment of a catalog item to run a Flow Designer flow when submitted. Where is this attachment configured?

options.text: On the catalog item, set the flow as the item's fulfillment flow/workflow.
On the user's profile.
In the user's browser settings.
On the change_request table's number-maintenance record.

rationale: Each catalog item points at the flow (or older Workflow) that fulfills it. Submission triggers the bound flow with the variable answers as inputs.

distractor_notes.B: User profile doesn't dictate catalog fulfillment.
distractor_notes.C: Browser settings don't run server-side flows.
distractor_notes.D: Number maintenance configures record numbering, not flows.

stem: Incident, Problem, and Change all share fields like Number, State, and Assigned to. Which design makes this possible?

options.text: They all extend the base Task table and inherit its fields
Each table independently re-creates identical fields
A transform map copies fields between them nightly
They share one physical row per record

rationale: Incident, Problem, Change, and Catalog Task all extend the Task table, inheriting its common fields (number, state, assigned_to, priority) and adding their own. That shared parent is why task-type records feel consistent across ITSM.

distractor_notes.B: Re-creating fields per table would defeat inheritance and cause drift.
distractor_notes.C: No nightly copy is involved — it's table extension/inheritance.
distractor_notes.D: Each record is its own row; extension shares schema, not rows.

stem: An agent needs to record internal troubleshooting that the customer should NOT see on the portal. Which field should they use?

options.text: Work notes
Additional comments
Short description
Description

rationale: Work notes are the internal, agent-facing journal; Additional comments (customer-visible) are what the requester sees. Internal-only detail belongs in work notes.

distractor_notes.B: Additional comments are customer-visible — exactly what to avoid here.
distractor_notes.C: Short description is the public summary of the issue.
distractor_notes.D: Description is also generally visible and not the internal journal.

stem: A low-risk, repeatable change (like a routine password policy update) is pre-approved and follows a template. Which change type is this?

options.text: Standard change
Normal change
Emergency change
Problem

rationale: Standard changes are pre-approved, low-risk, and template-driven — no CAB needed each time. Normal changes go through full assessment and approval; emergency changes are expedited for urgent fixes.

distractor_notes.B: Normal changes require full risk assessment and approval, not pre-approval.
distractor_notes.C: Emergency changes are for urgent, unplanned fixes.
distractor_notes.D: A problem investigates root cause; it isn't a change type.

stem: A server outage requires an immediate fix outside the normal approval timeline. Which change type applies?

options.text: Emergency change
Standard change
Normal change
Knowledge article

rationale: Emergency changes handle urgent situations (like outages) with an expedited approval path so the fix isn't blocked by the normal cycle, while still being recorded for review.

distractor_notes.B: Standard changes are pre-approved low-risk routines, not urgent fixes.
distractor_notes.C: Normal changes follow the full timeline — too slow for an outage.
distractor_notes.D: A knowledge article documents information; it isn't a change.

stem: Several incidents share the same recurring cause. Which record type is used to investigate and eliminate that underlying root cause?

options.text: Problem
Another incident
Change task
Knowledge base

rationale: Incidents restore service quickly; a Problem record investigates the root cause so the issue stops recurring. Linking the incidents to a problem is the standard pattern.

distractor_notes.B: Opening more incidents treats symptoms, not the root cause.
distractor_notes.C: A change implements a fix but isn't the root-cause investigation record.
distractor_notes.D: A knowledge base stores articles; it doesn't perform investigation.

stem: You need to restrict a knowledge base so only HR employees can read its articles. Which mechanism controls this access?

options.text: User criteria (can read / cannot read)
A coalesce field
A UI policy
A scheduled job

rationale: User criteria define who can read or contribute to a knowledge base (or catalog), based on attributes like role, group, department, or company. They're the access mechanism for knowledge and catalog content.

distractor_notes.B: Coalesce is an import-matching concept.
distractor_notes.C: UI policies change form fields, not knowledge access.
distractor_notes.D: Scheduled jobs run on timers, unrelated to read access.

stem: A draft knowledge article should be reviewed and approved before it becomes visible to readers. What governs this progression?

options.text: The knowledge workflow (draft to review to published)
A coalesce field
The list editor
A watch list

rationale: Knowledge articles move through a workflow — draft, review/approval, then published — so content is vetted before readers see it. Retirement/expiration can follow later in the lifecycle.

distractor_notes.B: Coalesce is unrelated to knowledge publishing.
distractor_notes.C: The list editor edits field values, not publishing state transitions.
distractor_notes.D: Watch lists notify people; they don't govern publication.

stem: An organization wants separate article collections for IT and HR, each with its own owners and access rules. How should this be structured?

options.text: Create separate knowledge bases, each with its own user criteria
Put everything in one base and rely on tags
Create one base and one giant article
Use update sets to separate them

rationale: Multiple knowledge bases let each group own its content and apply its own user criteria for read/contribute access — clean separation for IT vs HR. Tags alone wouldn't enforce access boundaries.

distractor_notes.B: Tags organize but don't enforce per-group access like user criteria on separate bases.
distractor_notes.C: One article can't represent two managed collections.
distractor_notes.D: Update sets move configuration; they don't structure knowledge access.

stem: On a Change record, you see related Change Tasks that must be completed as part of the change. What is the relationship between them?

options.text: The change is the parent; the change tasks are its children
They are unrelated records that happen to share a number
Each change task is a separate incident
The tasks are knowledge articles

rationale: Change tasks are child records of the parent change, breaking the work into trackable steps. Parent/child task relationships are a common ITSM pattern for coordinating multi-step work.

distractor_notes.B: They're explicitly related as parent/child, not coincidental.
distractor_notes.C: Change tasks extend Task but aren't incidents.
distractor_notes.D: They're tasks to perform, not knowledge articles.

stem: An agent has restored service for a caller and confirmed the fix works. Which incident state best reflects that the work is finished pending closure?

options.text: Resolved
New
On hold
In progress

rationale: Resolved indicates service is restored and the fix confirmed, typically before final Closed. New, In Progress, and On Hold all represent earlier points in the incident lifecycle.

distractor_notes.B: New is the just-logged state, before work begins.
distractor_notes.C: On Hold pauses work awaiting info or a third party.
distractor_notes.D: In Progress means work is actively underway, not finished.

stem: Which TWO statements about change types are correct?

options.text: Standard changes are pre-approved and template-based
Normal changes go through assessment and approval
Emergency changes require no record at all
Standard changes always require CAB approval each time

rationale: Standard changes are pre-approved templates for low-risk routine work; normal changes follow full assessment and approval. Emergency changes are still recorded, and standard changes specifically avoid per-instance CAB approval.

distractor_notes.C: Emergency changes are expedited but still recorded and reviewed.
distractor_notes.D: Standard changes are pre-approved precisely to avoid CAB each time.

stem: Which TWO are true about Knowledge Management?

options.text: User criteria control who can read or contribute to a knowledge base
Articles follow a workflow before being published
All knowledge bases are visible to every user by default and cannot be restricted
Knowledge articles must be stored in update sets

rationale: Knowledge access is governed by user criteria, and articles move through a publish workflow before going live. Access can be restricted, and articles are data, not configuration moved in update sets.

distractor_notes.C: User criteria can restrict read/contribute access per base.
distractor_notes.D: Articles are content/data, not update-set configuration.

stem: A user orders two items from the service catalog in one submission. What record structure is generated?

options.text: One Request (REQ) with a Requested Item (RITM) per item, each spawning catalog tasks
One incident per item
A single flat record with both items in one field
One change request

rationale: Catalog orders use a hierarchy: a Request (REQ) holds one Requested Item (RITM) per ordered item, and each RITM generates the catalog tasks needed to fulfill it. That structure tracks fulfillment item by item.

distractor_notes.B: Catalog orders create requests/RITMs, not incidents.
distractor_notes.C: Each item gets its own RITM, not a single merged field.
distractor_notes.D: A change request is for changes, not catalog fulfillment.

stem: You want a friendly catalog-style form that, when submitted, creates an Incident record on a non-catalog table. Which catalog object does this?

options.text: A record producer
A standard catalog item
An order guide
A variable set

rationale: A record producer is a catalog interface that creates a record on a target table (like Incident) from a simplified, guided form. Regular catalog items generate requests/RITMs rather than writing directly to another table.

distractor_notes.B: A standard catalog item produces a request/RITM, not a direct record on another table.
distractor_notes.C: Order guides bundle multiple items; they don't create a single target record.
distractor_notes.D: A variable set is a reusable group of variables, not a producer.

stem: Five catalog items all need the same block of 'employee details' questions. What's the most maintainable way to share them?

options.text: Build a variable set and attach it to each item
Re-create the variables on each item
Use a coalesce field
Add the questions to a knowledge article

rationale: A variable set is a reusable group of variables you attach to multiple catalog items — define once, reuse everywhere, and update in one place. Re-creating variables per item causes duplication and drift.

distractor_notes.B: Duplicating variables is exactly what variable sets avoid.
distractor_notes.C: Coalesce is an import concept, unrelated to catalog variables.
distractor_notes.D: Knowledge articles document info; they don't collect catalog input.

stem: New-hire onboarding should let a manager order a laptop, phone, and access in one guided flow. Which catalog feature fits best?

options.text: An order guide
A single catalog item
A record producer
A knowledge base

rationale: Order guides walk a requester through ordering multiple related items together (and can pass shared answers between them), which is ideal for onboarding bundles. A single item couldn't represent the full bundle.

distractor_notes.B: One catalog item covers one thing, not a multi-item bundle.
distractor_notes.C: A record producer creates one record on a table, not a multi-item order.
distractor_notes.D: A knowledge base stores articles, not orderable bundles.

stem: On a catalog item, a 'Manager name' variable should appear only when the user selects 'Requesting for someone else.' Which tool changes variable behavior dynamically?

options.text: A catalog UI policy
An ACL
A transform map
A scheduled job

rationale: Catalog UI policies make catalog variables dynamically mandatory, visible, or read-only based on other selections — exactly the show-on-condition behavior here. ACLs handle security, not form dynamics.

distractor_notes.B: ACLs control access, not show/hide logic on a variable.
distractor_notes.C: Transform maps move imported data, not catalog form behavior.
distractor_notes.D: Scheduled jobs run on timers, unrelated to variable visibility.

stem: A catalog item for VPN access should only be orderable by full-time employees. Which mechanism restricts who can see and order it?

options.text: User criteria on the catalog item
A coalesce field
A watch list
The list editor

rationale: Just like knowledge, catalog visibility is governed by user criteria — define who can (or cannot) see and order an item based on role, group, department, and so on.

distractor_notes.B: Coalesce is for import matching, not catalog access.
distractor_notes.C: Watch lists notify people; they don't restrict ordering.
distractor_notes.D: The list editor edits field values, not access.

stem: After an RITM is approved, fulfillment requires several steps handled by different teams. What records coordinate that work?

options.text: Catalog tasks (sc_task) generated from the RITM
Additional incidents
Knowledge articles
Update sets

rationale: Catalog tasks (sc_task) are the fulfillment steps spawned from a Requested Item, assignable to the teams that complete each part of the order. They sit below the RITM in the request hierarchy.

distractor_notes.B: Incidents track service disruptions, not catalog fulfillment steps.
distractor_notes.C: Knowledge articles document information; they don't fulfill orders.
distractor_notes.D: Update sets carry configuration between instances.

stem: To help users find items, a catalog should organize items into browsable groupings like 'Hardware' and 'Software.' What provides this organization?

options.text: Catalog categories
Coalesce fields
Watch lists
Dictionary overrides

rationale: Categories group catalog items into browsable sections so users can find what they need. They're the structural navigation layer within a catalog.

distractor_notes.B: Coalesce is an import-matching concept.
distractor_notes.C: Watch lists handle notifications.
distractor_notes.D: Dictionary overrides change field behavior on extended tables.

stem: A catalog item needs a dropdown whose choices come from records on the User table. Which variable type is appropriate?

options.text: A Reference variable pointing at the User table
A single-line text variable
A checkbox variable
A label

rationale: A Reference variable lets users pick an existing record (such as a user) from a target table, keeping the selection valid and linked. Free text or a checkbox can't enforce a real record selection.

distractor_notes.B: Free text doesn't constrain input to actual user records.
distractor_notes.C: A checkbox is a yes/no toggle, not a record picker.
distractor_notes.D: A label displays text and collects no input.

stem: A requester wants to know why their order isn't complete yet. Where do you look to see the per-item fulfillment progress?

options.text: The Requested Item (RITM) and its catalog tasks
The parent Request's number only
A knowledge article
The update set log

rationale: The RITM shows the status of that specific item, and its catalog tasks reveal which fulfillment steps are done or pending. The parent REQ summarizes, but the detail lives at the RITM/task level.

distractor_notes.B: The REQ number alone summarizes; it doesn't show per-step progress.
distractor_notes.C: Knowledge articles don't track an individual order.
distractor_notes.D: Update set logs track configuration moves, not order fulfillment.

stem: Which TWO statements about the Service Catalog request model are correct?

options.text: A Request (REQ) can contain multiple Requested Items (RITMs)
Catalog tasks (sc_task) carry out the fulfillment steps for an RITM
A record producer always generates a Request and RITM
Catalog items can never be restricted by audience

rationale: The model nests REQ > RITM > catalog task, with tasks doing the fulfillment work. Record producers instead create a record on a target table, and catalog items can be restricted via user criteria.

distractor_notes.C: A record producer creates a target-table record, not a REQ/RITM.
distractor_notes.D: User criteria can restrict who sees and orders a catalog item.

stem: Which TWO are valid ways to reuse or control catalog content?

options.text: Attach a variable set to multiple catalog items
Use a catalog UI policy to make a variable conditionally mandatory
Use a coalesce field to hide a variable
Use a scheduled job to validate a variable on submit

rationale: Variable sets share variables across items, and catalog UI policies control variable behavior (mandatory/visible/read-only) dynamically. Coalesce and scheduled jobs are unrelated to catalog form logic.

distractor_notes.C: Coalesce matches records on import; it doesn't hide variables.
distractor_notes.D: Scheduled jobs run on timers; on-submit variable validation uses catalog client scripts/UI policies.
